report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

When we use a measure 𝑋 for some hypothesized variable of the natural world 𝑇 𝑋 that is not directly observable (i.e., latent), then that measure will depend on some function 𝑔 of one or more indicators from that natural world 𝐼 𝑋 .

For example, when using an infrared ear thermometer, the goal is to measure core temperature 𝑇 𝑋 as indicated by infrared light 𝐼 𝑋 , which is transformed within the thermometer by a known function 𝑔 to yield the measure of temperature 𝑋.

When there is little error, such a procedure may yield measures that are very close to the true values (𝑋 ≈ 𝑇 𝑋 ), and that make it more or less unproblematic to use those measures as if they directly correspond to the true variables.

However, if the indicators 𝐼 𝑋 only capture 𝑇 𝑋 imprecisely, so that the measure 𝑋 has some substantial error, then that will bias the estimates of the latent variable, and, in turn, that variable's relationship with other variables, unless the measure is defined in a way so that error is accounted for.
Errors are often unaccounted when psychological researchers take their measurements.

For example, if peoples' perception or cognition, or the measurement instrument itself, only has the precision to report a truly continuous trait (𝑇 𝑋 ) through some discrete categories (e.g., "a lot", "strongly agree"), then even in the best-case scenario the indicator (𝐼 𝑋 ) can only specify a range of true values to which each indicator value is associated.
Therefore, there will be some error, however 𝑔 is specified.
Depending on the properties of the errors, this may bias various statistics.
In contrast, accounting for errors is regularly considered in sciences such as physics.

When a measurement is to be made, properties of the measurement situation and the measurement instrument are considered, and the instrument is fine-tuned in each specific situation to ensure errors are small enough for purposes of the measurement.
There are certainly many statistical methods for handling various errors.

However, these methods are often specialized to a particular type of application, which means a more general consideration of errors can be beyond the scope of most applied researchers, beyond the methods in which they have had special training.
These methods also often treat measurement and statistical modelling of errors separately, which may explain why measurement without statistical modelling of errors remains common.
Contrast this with the procedure above, where it is recognized that modelling and handling errors is required before measurements are taken, and that this is to affect how measurements are scored.

Developing a general model of how to define functions 𝑔 from a set of indicators 𝐼 𝑋 , based on an error model, can hopefully aid psychological researchers in incorporating error modelling into their general analysis procedure with greater regularity.
The goal with this paper is to develop principles for functions 𝑔 and corresponding scorings for 𝑋 that avoid bias in latent linear models for a wide category of errors.

In particular, also for errors for which it is not possible to define a measurement decomposition as in Classical Test Theory (CTT): 𝑋 = 𝑇 𝑋 + 𝜀 𝑋 such that 𝐸(𝜀 𝑋 |𝑇 𝑋 = 𝑡) = 0 for all values 𝑡 of 𝑇; and for errors for which the Item Response Theory (IRT) assumption about local independence is not fulfilled.
This will lead to a novel way of estimating regression parameters under various error structures through the same general steps.
We return to some further advantages of this method in the Discussion.

The variables we observe that, together with an appropriate measurement model, provide some information about the true variables.
By design, we define the indicators very broadly so that they may represent various types of observations and measurement issues.
If 𝑇 𝑋 is observed directly, then 𝐼 𝑋 = 𝑇 𝑋 .
If data is sometimes missing for 𝑇 𝑋 , then 𝐼 𝑋 = 𝑇 𝑋 when 𝑇 𝑋 is observed, and 𝐼 𝑋 = "𝑁𝐴" otherwise.

text.text: We now discuss how two special methods can be understood as prediction decompositions aimed at preserving the linear relationship.
We present these as seeing them can help with understanding the broad applicability of this type of scoring.

First, Berkson (1950) considered how repeated manipulations of a predictor (measurably) set to the same level may produce random errors around this level when that exact level is not perfectly controlled for.

text.text: As shown by Berkson, when the errors around the measurement values for a single predictor are truly randomand so, when a prediction decomposition for that sole predictor is fulfilledthen the linear relationship will be retained.
As an example, say that researchers study the effect of a nutrition compound on plant height using two groups, one not given the nutrition, and one given it.
Say there are n plants in each group and that k grams of the nutrition are given to the experimental group.

Now, if the effect is linear (for the included range of nutrition), then even if some plants in the experimental condition happen to get more of the nutrition than other plants then this will not bias the estimate of the effect, which is still 𝛽 0 in the control group, and 𝛽 0 + 𝛽 1 * 𝑘 𝑛 ⁄ in the experimental group.

Second, in typical instrumental variables methods (see Pearl, 2000), the measured predictor of interest (we only consider one predictor) has an unwanted correlation with the regression error term 𝜖 that cannot be handled by including further control variables.

text.text: Instead, one assumes there exists a so-called instrumental variable, which can linearly predict the predictor of interest in such a way that none of the variation in common with the error term 𝜖 is included in those linear predictions (this works when the instrumental variable has no correlation with the outcome beyond its correlation with the predictor of interest).

These linear predictions then (asymptotically) fulfill an unbiased prediction decomposition, where the predicted values from the instrumental variable act as 𝑋, and the part of the predictor of interest that is not correlated with the error term acts as 𝑇 𝑋.

As such, it can provide a more general type of scoring for preserving latent linear relationships.

Researchers may then need to look for other methods, or other ways of measuring so that the error of 𝑻 𝑿 no longer depends on 𝑇 𝑌.

Alternatively, the Error assumption (17) may not be fulfilled because the errors of 𝑻 𝑿 depend on some unincluded predictors (the difference to the case above is that 𝑿 may now only depend on a subset of the variance in 𝜖, while if 𝑿 depends on 𝑇 𝑌 directly, then it depends on all the variance in 𝜖).
We may compare this to having an omitted predictor that is correlated with the included predictors 𝑻 𝑿 .
This will lead to biased OLS parameters compared to if it had been included.

When we have measures 𝑿 of 𝑻 𝑿 , these could correlate with the error 𝜖 both because 𝑻 𝑿 are correlated with unincluded variables, but also because the error of 𝑻 𝑿 , that causes it to have a certain measure-score for 𝑿, could be correlated with such variables.
Consequently, just like we should include such variables amongst our predictors 𝑻 𝑿 without errors, we should include a potentially larger set of such variables amongst our predictors 𝑿 with errors.

If we can do so (without including further dependencies on unincluded variables), then the error of the predictors will now be covered by our extended set of predictors 𝑻 𝑿 , and we can apply Theorem 1 again.
Note also, although this is rarely fulfilled in practice, that if our set of included true predictors 𝑻 𝑿 perfectly predict 𝑇 𝑌 (so 𝜖 = 0), then Assumption 2 is trivially fulfilled.
Versions of the Error assumption (Assumption 2) are assumed in various methods, albeit often indirectly, as we further note in Table 1 below.

By "random" it is meant that they are not associated with other sources of variance, including 𝜖.
Therefore, the Error assumption is fulfilled.
Similarly, in instrumental variables methods the instrumental variable 𝑍 is assumed to not have any association with the outcome 𝑇 𝑌 beyond what is explained by 𝑇 𝑋 .
This is just a statement that the predictions 𝑋 based on 𝑍 (𝑋 = 𝐸(𝑇 𝑋 |𝑍)) are not going to be associated with 𝜖.
Thus, again, the Error assumption is fulfilled.

If this is slow, a numerical minimization of the (squared) difference between initial and updated values can also be used (this can be especially useful if parameters are inbetween some highest and lowest values, e.g., ±1).

If an analytical formula is available, that can be used directly.
Alternatively, expectations may be solved numerically, or estimated through simulation by repeated draws from the population model implied by the parameters.

Step 2.1: Estimate further nuisance parameters for 𝑌 that need to take into account the predictor 𝑿-variables, if necessary (note that we can do this if needed, as we only required that 𝜽 could be estimated independently of the outcome, not the predictors).

Then regress 𝑌 onto the 𝑿-variables from Step 1.2, update the 𝜷-estimates in some appropriate way, calculate new expected values for 𝑌, and repeat until convergence.

Theorem 2 justifies estimation by the 2x2 Em iterative plugin procedure above.
While this may yield asymptotically correct estimates when the assumptions are fulfilled, we should also consider how to estimate the sampling error of the estimation procedure.

In general, the procedure above contains two sources of increased sampling error compared to if variables could have been measured without any error: (I) the extra residual error from the 𝜀 𝑌 , 𝜺 𝑿 errors themselves, and (II) the extra sampling error from having to estimate the expected values and nuisance parameters.
The model in Theorem 1 is expressed very generally, so we should also consider general ways to estimate this sampling error.
Large-sample errors could be possible to derive, potentially from earlier methods when the methods can be shown to converge.

Estimation should also be possible to accomplish by utilizing Bootstrapped standard errors (Efron, 1979), where the Em estimation procedure is resampled with replacement, and where the variation across samples is used to estimate the standard error.

text.text: Using Bootstrapped standard errors has one advantage related to each point (I)-(II) above.
(I) The errors 𝜀 𝑌 , 𝜺 𝑿 are unlikely to be independent and normally distributed, even if this is true for 𝜖, so the total residual error for the measurements will not have a normal distribution.
Bootstrapping allows accounting for this non-normality.

(II) When the expected values and nuisance parameters need to be estimated in the sample (as they usually need to be), the usual residuals from the OLS regression will not capture this extra uncertainty as it is only applied once those estimates are plugged in.
Bootstrapping the full Em estimation procedure allows accounting for the sampling error that comes from this extra uncertainty.

Here we derived a population model about errors that allowed latent linear relationships to be retained (Theorem 1), and a corresponding estimation method (Theorem 2).
We showed how this can be used both to estimate such latent linear relationships, or to estimate nonlinear relationships between observed variables through the use of pseudo-latent variables.

We also showed variance ratios that, like reliabilities, can function as measures of the precisions of our measures, and that can be used to quantify the change in explained variance between latent and observed variables, and to evaluate the usefulness of modelling that error.

The model we derived is also more general than prior models for retaining latent linear relationships (Lu & Thomas, 2008; Skrondal & Laake, 2001), as indicated by Lemma 1-2, as we also score the outcome by an unbiased prediction decomposition.

text.text: The model and its related Em estimation method also has several practical advantages.
First, when estimating the 𝜷-parameters the 𝑿 𝑇 𝑿 matrix technically only needs to be inverted once.
This may speed up estimation when this matrix is large.
The reason for this is that for each OLS iteration, we are estimating with (𝑿 𝜽 T𝑿 𝜽 ̂)-1 𝑿 𝜽 T𝑌 𝜽 ̂,𝜷 ̂, and 𝑌 𝜽 ̂,𝜷 ̂ the is the only part that needs to be updated based on the new estimates of 𝜷.
Although it may of course be advantageous to introduce an iterative weight matrix into these estimates, especially when the variance of 𝑌 𝜽 ̂,𝜷 ̂|𝑿 𝜽 ̂=𝒙 varies a lot for different 𝒙.
The fact that we define the scores for the predictors and the outcome in a corresponding way may also yield certain benefits.
Consider if the scores need to be estimated in a chained way.
That is, where scores for predictors also depend on other predictors.
If those scores can be estimated through the Em algorithm, then we can start with the estimates that need the least predictors.
Once we have 𝜷-estimates in that relationship, this gives us a complete expression for the joint distribution of those 𝑿-variables, say for the first 𝑗 predictors.
We can then use this directly in a second step, where these variables predict the 𝑗 + 1:th predictor.
This is then repeated until we arrive at predicting the outcome 𝑌.

The fact that we can use similar steps (by the Em algorithm) to estimate various types of errors is also advantageous, in that it can aid researchers in considering a larger variety of errors with more regularity.

In all cases, we start with a measurement model, consider if, and if so, how nuisance parameters 𝜽 can be estimated separately from the 𝜷-parameters, evaluate and potentially modify the measurement and/or the number of predictors so that the measured predictors should not depend on the regression error term 𝜖 (this concerns dependence both for the true predictors and for their indicators), estimate 𝜽-parameters that do not depend on any joint predictors, calculate the expected values of the predictors (possibly in a chained way) and potential further 𝜽-parameters that require considering the joint distribution of the predictors (including intercepts and slopes between the predictors), and then estimate the expected values for the outcome and the 𝜷-parameters iteratively.
The steps always concern ensuring Assumption 1-4 are fulfilled, finding expected values for the predictors, and then using those to estimate expected values and OLS parameters for the outcome.

As we split up the estimation into parts, this may further enable researchers to derive models for their errors, as they can first consider a model of the nuisance parameters, then the predictors (which itself can be broken up into steps), and then the outcome, which may be simpler than modelling a joint distribution all at once.
Additionally, as multiple errors can be considered through the same steps, it can hopefully aid researchers in considering joint types of errors in the same model, as in Example 3.
The focus on expected-value scores also enables estimating scores by simulation even in cases where deriving those expectations is otherwise difficult.
This will not be as quick as otherwise, but it can be utilized as a brute force approach even in complicated models.

Relatedly, the focus of expected values of the true variables conditional on the indicators, and the fact that each such score leads to no direct requirement for other scores (by the derivation in Lemma 2), means that if we can define a joint distribution of the true variables and indicators, then we can apply that directly to derive the scores without needing to solve an equation of other scores.

This can make scores according to our prediction decomposition easier to apply in practice, even when both types of scores can be defined, which means that applying them further, such as in the simulations of expected values discussed above, can be easier to do in practice as well.
This could potentially also make it simpler to apply in programming packages that calculate such scores under flexible types of distributions.
The method that has been presented here thus appears highly applicable and flexible.
However, some limitations of the current treatment should be noted.
First, the flexibility of the method means that it can be applied in different ways even for the same problem.

This can be an advantage (e.g., one method may be possible to apply under conditions when another cannot), but it also means that new applications should check so that the proposed method has good properties compared to other methods.
In the logistic regression part of Example 2, we used two different methods, and showed that they had converged on the right relationship.
However, if one of the methods yields estimates with consistently lower standard errors than another, then that first method should clearly be preferred.
Both may be versions of the method we apply, so, certainly, checks should also be applied to ensure each particular application works satisfactorily.
In a similar vein, our Theorem 2 provides conditions to ensure the iterative updating will asymptotically move the conditional expectations in the correct direction for each iteration.
However, any new application should modify the updating and check so that estimates converge as expected.

The updated expectations may differ very little, making the iterative updating very slow unless some speedup is included, or (if (43) is not fulfilled), differ too much unless the updating is slowed down.

Theorem 2 provides a flexible result about the direction in which expectations should be updated, how far that each iteration should update in that direction should be tailored to each problem at hand.
It should also be studied how some of our assumptions could be relaxed.
Assumption 1-2 are fairly open, and Assumption 3-4 also holds under many cases, but there are also cases where they do not.
Assumption 4 might be relaxed to an assumption that the covariances 𝐶𝑜𝑣(𝑿 1:𝑝,𝜽 ̂, 𝑌 𝜽 ̂,𝜷 ̂) (and, if necessary, the expectations) move in the correct direction when estimates are updated.
Again, this is because we are keeping the same 𝐶𝑜𝑣(𝑿 1:𝑝,𝜽 ̂) matrix at each iteration.
Therefore, the estimates of the slopes (𝐶𝑜𝑣(𝑿 1:𝑝,𝜽 ̂)) -1 𝐶𝑜𝑣(𝑿 1:𝑝,𝜽 ̂, 𝑌 𝜽 ̂,𝜷 ̂) will move in the right direction.
This may also yield a way to soften (43) without needing to account for overshooting.
Because even if expectations for some 𝒙 change quicker than indicated by (43), it may be that others change slower, and that this balances out in the covariance as a whole.
The model of measurement errors presented in Theorem 1 provides a broad analytical model for considering and handling various errors.
As shown by Lemma 2, the scores of Theorem 1 can be applied for a wide variety of errors.
The analytical model derived in Theorem 1 is useful on its own in that it can be used to understand the consequences of errors.

Even where expectations are not possible to estimate, or where the estimation procedure suggested here is less efficient, it can provide understanding about the optimal scores that would be required to avoid bias, and how much this could differ from the scores used by researchers.
It can also hopefully enable communicating the consequences of a broader set of errors.
Finally, we derived a novel way to estimate OLS parameters through an Em algorithm in Theorem 2 for the multiple models that fulfill or can be made to fulfill the structure in Theorem 1.

Future studies should further examine the general behavior of the algorithm, and how to specify the algorithm to estimate expected values and nuisance parameters most effectively for various measurements.
The model also provides the possibility of deriving flexible code for estimating these models using the same general steps under various errors structures and distributions.

We present this example in detail in the Supplemental Materials and summarize it here.
Here we evaluate how multiple types of errors can be modelled at once using Theorem 1-2 and the Em algorithm, and how prior/population information can be used to estimate the expected values.
Specifically, we predict political interest with the main effects of sex and age (which was fairly linear, and not dependent on the interaction).

We introduce errors in all three variables: misclassification in the sex variable (can e.g., be the case if it has been estimated from some online or textual indicators), dichotomization of the age variable, and missing data in the political interest variable, which would be MAR dependent upon the sex of participants if we could observe it without error.

We show how to formulate the expected values in our model, and how we can use governmental data about sex and age to estimate the expected values using the proportion of men and women and the age distribution, together with information in the sample about the sensitivity and specificity of the sex indicator and the proportion in the dichotomized age variable.

As missingness in political interest is dependent on the true sex of participants, and as we only observe the indicator with a risk of misclassification, we further incorporate this in the expected values for the missing cases.
Finally, we also use the variance ratios from Corollary 1-2 to evaluate whether it would serve to treat the original age-variable (measured with integers), as an indicator of a latent true age.

As the corresponding variance ratio (the precision), can be shown to be very close to one, so that the difference in the error due to this lack of precision is very marginal (per Corollary 1), we have a marker that can show us that modelling this is likely not all that necessary, provided bias is avoided.
We can therefore focus on modelling more severe types of errors.
Calculations for the expected values are presented in Appendix E3 at the end of this file.
Here we show how population information, or information from a prior dataset, can be used to estimate the expected values.
We also show how misclassified variables, thresholded variables, and variables with missing data can be modelled using Theorem 1 and the 2x2 Em algorithm.
This example also illustrates a case where no iterative updating of the outcome is required.
Finally, we show how the variance ratios of Corollary 2 can be used to evaluate the (non)importance of modelling certain errors.
Missing data that is MAR conditional on the true sex of participants requires no separate parameter, but affects the expected values.
